entries.content:
CAPTCHAs are something most of us have come across while browsing the internet. Sometimes we're asked to identify traffic lights in pictures, solve a small puzzle, or simply tick a box to confirm we're human. Websites use these challenges to help distinguish real users from automated bots.

But there's an interesting problem with this approach. What happens when a bot doesn't need to solve the CAPTCHA itself because a real person can solve it for them?

This is how CAPTCHA farms work. Attackers use services where real people solve CAPTCHA challenges on behalf of automated programs. The person completing the challenge is human, but the activity happening behind it may still be controlled by a bot. This makes it harder for websites to identify suspicious requests, even when their CAPTCHA system appears to be working correctly.

Here, we'll look at how CAPTCHA farm attacks work, why attackers use human solvers, and what makes these attacks difficult to detect. We'll also go through some of the security measures developers can use to identify suspicious activity and better protect their websites.

What We'll Cover:

What Is a CAPTCHA Farm Attack?

To understand how these attacks work, it helps to distinguish between the two primary ways attackers deal with verification gates: machine-driven recognition and human-driven outsourcing.

In an automated CAPTCHA-solving attack, an attacker uses computer vision models, optical character recognition (OCR), or neural networks to parse the challenge image and guess the answer without human intervention.

This approach is fast and computationally cheap, but it frequently fails when security vendors update their visual distortions, introduce interactive logic puzzles, or assess human-like mouse kinematics.

A CAPTCHA farm attack takes the opposite route. Instead of attempting to outsmart the defensive algorithm with software, the attacker routes the challenge to a human solving service. These commercial operations maintain large networks of manual workers who solve puzzles continuously around the clock. By inserting a human into the loop, the attacker converts what should be a technical roadblock into an outsourced labor pipeline.

The attack doesn't break the cryptography or reverse-engineer the underlying challenge code. Instead, it relies on a CAPTCHA relay attack: software manages the speed and scale of the attack, while real human eyes provide the cognitive validation the website expects.

Behind the Scenes: The Four-Part Infrastructure

A functional CAPTCHA farm is neither an ad-hoc group of rogue hackers nor an obscure black-box script. It's a commercial, multi-tiered infrastructure built around standard web development protocols.

Four distinct components work together to make the relay happen in a matter of seconds.

First is the attacker’s automated script. This client bot typically runs headlessly via browser automation tools like Puppeteer, Playwright, or custom HTTP client libraries. The script navigates to a target platform, such as a user registration portal, and fills in usernames, passwords, and demographic fields at machine speed until it hits a defensive challenge.

Second is the CAPTCHA-solving platform's API. Commercial solver platforms act as brokers between abuse operators and manual laborers. When the attacker's script encounters a challenge, it intercepts the site's public key, the challenge URL, and the visual assets, packaging them into an HTTP POST request directed at the solving service’s application programming interface (API).

Third is the distributed human workforce. Workers access these services through dedicated web dashboards, mobile apps, or browser plug-ins. When the API receives a task from an attacker, it pushes the image directly onto a worker’s screen. The worker identifies the bicycles or fire hydrants, types the distorted characters, or drags the puzzle slider into place, earning a microscopic payout, often ranging from $0.50 to $2.00 per thousand puzzles solved.

Fourth is the payload delivery back to the target. Once the worker submits the correct solution, the broker API returns the generated verification token back to the attacker’s script. The script injects this validation token into the target website's hidden form field and fires the final submission request. To the receiving server, the request bears an authentic verification signature generated by a real human session.

How an Attack Unfolds: A Step-by-Step Look

To see how these parts interact in practice, consider a credential-stuffing or mass-account registration campaign against an online service.

  • Initiation: The attacker's script dispatches an HTTP request to establish a session with the target registration page, populating the input fields with generated credentials.
  • Challenge trigger: The target application evaluates the incoming request. Detecting an unfamiliar IP address or an incomplete browser fingerprint, it triggers a CAPTCHA modal, pausing the registration sequence until a valid solution token is supplied.
  • Extraction and dispatch: The bot reads the page DOM, captures the puzzle iframe parameters, site key, and challenge payload, and forwards this data to the CAPTCHA farm API.
  • Human execution: The farm's queuing system allocates the challenge to an active human worker. The worker completes the puzzle within an average response window of 10 to 25 seconds.
  • Token retrieval: The worker’s response yields an official validation token from the CAPTCHA provider's origin server. The solving farm's API returns this signed string to the attacker’s script.
  • Form finalization: The script injects the token into the page's response payload (such as g-recaptcha-response) and submits the form. The website’s backend queries the CAPTCHA provider's verification API, receives a confirmation that the challenge was successfully passed, and creates the account.

The entire loop completes well before typical session timeouts kick in, leaving the target server with no obvious visual anomaly to flag.

Why Attackers Rely on Human Solvers

Building and maintaining custom neural networks to break modern visual challenges requires constant development effort. Defensive providers frequently alter noise patterns, camera angles, distortion algorithms and semantic puzzles specifically to break automated image classifiers.

Human solvers bypass this arms race entirely because the human visual cortex processes semantic context effortlessly. A person instantly understands what constitutes a "motorcycle," even if the image is cropped awkwardly, partially obscured by street foliage, or rendered under strange lighting.

This human adaptability is supported by extensive security research. In a foundational study, Towards Understanding the Security of Modern Image Captchas and Underground Captcha-Solving Services, researchers analyzed the commercial ecosystem across 152 solving platforms. They found that human-solving services achieved near-flawless accuracy rates across complex, diverse image challenges where purely automated computer vision solvers repeatedly struggled or degraded over time.

Outsourcing the problem is also remarkably inexpensive. Because labor pools are drawn from regions with low living costs, attackers can bypass thousands of protective checkpoints for less than the price of a cup of coffee. The workflow is highly scalable: software handles millions of connections, while human labor is summoned on-demand only for the few seconds required to clear a barrier.

What CAPTCHA Farms Target

CAPTCHA farms rarely serve as self-contained attacks. Instead, they act as an operational enabler for wider abusive campaigns across the web.

First, they enable mass fake account creation. Malicious actors generate millions of disposable profiles on social media, dating networks, and developer platforms to distribute phishing links, spam search engines, or run coordinated disinformation campaigns.

They also facilitate credential stuffing. When attackers test databases of leaked usernames and passwords against banking or retail portals, defensive systems usually throw a CAPTCHA after a handful of failed attempts. Solver APIs allow the credential-testing bots to continue cycling through login credentials uninterrupted.

Inventory hoarding and scalping is another common use case. High-demand retail drops, concert tickets, and travel bookings are frequent targets. Security researchers tracking real-world bot traffic at DataDome documented an operation where an attacker combined bot automation with a CAPTCHA farm to orchestrate 18 million automated ticket-scalping attempts, successfully bypassing front-line interactive verification.

And they enable data scraping at scale. Web crawlers harvesting competitive pricing, directory databases, or intellectual property frequently utilize solver APIs whenever protected search and discovery pages present challenge gates.

In every case, the CAPTCHA farm doesn't execute the underlying abuse: it merely removes the specific verification tripwire meant to halt it.

Why These Attacks Are Difficult to Stop

Stopping CAPTCHA farms is inherently difficult because they exploit the core assumption behind standard challenge-response security: that the entity answering the challenge is the entity making the request.

This systemic blind spot is analyzed in the research paper On the Security and Usability of Dynamic Cognitive Game CAPTCHAs, which evaluated how puzzle formats hold up against relay systems. The study demonstrated that regardless of how cognitively engaging, gamified, or technically dynamic a test is, relay architectures successfully decouple cognitive processing from the requesting client. The server receives a mathematically legitimate, human-generated solution token, making the puzzle itself effectively irrelevant.

Also, attackers route their client requests through residential proxy networks. The initial HTTP request comes from one residential IP address, the CAPTCHA is rendered by an automated browser mimicking common hardware profiles, and the solution is completed remotely. The defender’s server can't verify the physical proximity between the solver and the requesting client, creating an asymmetric advantage for the attacker.

How Websites Can Defend Themselves

Because human solvers can easily clear visual and cognitive challenges, treating a solved puzzle as a blanket guarantee of trustworthiness is no longer a viable defensive strategy. Web applications require a defense-in-depth model that monitors behaviors before, during, and long after a verification challenge appears.

Behavioral Telemetry and Biometrics

Automated scripts can easily spoof screen resolutions and user-agent strings, but reproducing organic human cursor movement across an entire page requires far more work. Real users demonstrate micro-deviations, variable acceleration curves, pauses, and continuous mouse tremors.

When a CAPTCHA farm attack takes place, there's often a distinct behavioral mismatch: the form fields are filled out instantaneously or via scripted keyboard events, followed by an abrupt pause while the remote worker solves the puzzle, followed by an instantaneous token injection. Monitoring telemetry across the whole lifecycle of the page exposes this artificial stitching.

Network and Device Fingerprinting

Defenders must assess context beyond the single page interaction. Inspecting TCP/IP packet behavior, TLS fingerprints (JA3/JA4 fingerprints), HTTP/2 frame parameters, and device APIs reveals whether the underlying runtime environment is a standard consumer browser or an orchestrated automation tool running inside a data center.

Modern Rate-Limiting Models

Relying entirely on puzzle solving often introduces accessibility barriers for real users while doing little to stop funded attackers. As explored in research published by the Association for Computing Machinery regarding mCaptcha and Proof-of-Work Rate Limiting, defensive architectures can enforce cryptographic proof of work puzzles at the transport layer.

By forcing the connecting client's CPU to compute complex mathematical problems proportional to the platform's current traffic load, defense systems raise the economic and computational cost of running automated campaigns, neutralizing attacks without demanding manual human puzzle-solving.

Post-Authentication Anomaly Detection

Passing an authentication challenge should never grant unconditional trust. Web architectures should monitor post-login activity for anomalous actions:

  • Does an account immediately attempt hundreds of data queries per minute right after registering?
  • Does it immediately navigate directly to high-value purchase endpoints without loading associated asset stylesheets or images?
  • Does the session change IP ranges and geographic locations between the initial page load and the final transaction?

Identifying these signals allows security teams to invalidate sessions even if the initial challenge was solved cleanly.

Security Beyond the Checkbox

CAPTCHA farms show why websites can't rely on a single security check to keep automated attacks away. Even when someone successfully completes a CAPTCHA, the request may still be part of an automated operation.

CAPTCHAs are designed to check whether a person can solve a particular challenge. But they can't tell whether that person is the actual user trying to access the website or someone solving the challenge on behalf of a bot. This is one of the reasons CAPTCHA farms can bypass a security measure that would normally stop automated traffic.

For developers, this means a completed CAPTCHA should be treated as just one part of the verification process. Websites also need to monitor user behavior, network activity, and suspicious requests to identify possible attacks. Combining these checks makes it easier to spot activity that a CAPTCHA alone might miss.

Conclusion

CAPTCHA farms make it difficult for websites to tell whether a completed verification challenge actually came from a legitimate user. Even when a real person solves the puzzle, the request may still be part of an automated attack.

For developers, this means it's worth paying attention to what happens before and after a CAPTCHA is completed. Things like unusual login attempts, repeated requests, unexpected changes in user behavior, and suspicious account activity can provide useful clues.

Using CAPTCHA alongside rate limiting, behavioral monitoring, and other security checks can help websites identify these attacks more effectively. It's also important to review these protections regularly as attackers change how they operate.

entries.title: Introducing Socrates and the New freeCodeCamp Forum
entries.summary: freeCodeCamp just turned 12 years old. And so did our beloved forum. And today I'm thrilled to say that the forum is now focused on discussions rather than Q&A. This is thanks to Socrates, a new tool
entries.content:
freeCodeCamp just turned 12 years old. And so did our beloved forum. And today I'm thrilled to say that the forum is now focused on discussions rather than Q&A.

This is thanks to Socrates, a new tool we just launched. Socrates is built right into the freeCodeCamp curriculum. It can look at your code and give you hints to help you get unstuck.

When you ask Socrates for help, first it references the thousands of hints and test cases we've human-authored for the curriculum. And if none of those cover your situation, Socrates will come up with new hints to guide you.

Here're some photos of Socrates in action:

Socrates is live now. Try it on the freeCodeCamp curriculum.

Socrates frees up the forum to serve as a place for discussions

Since most people will be getting unstuck using Socrates, we think far fewer people will need to ask for help on the forum. So we can instead use the forum as a place to talk with fellow human beings about our hobbies, passions, studies, and goals.

Over the years we've built up a super chill mod team. Folks from all over the world with a broad range of backgrounds. These knights and dames keep the vibe positive and productive, and keep out the bots and spammers.

So here's what I want you to do.

  • Read our 85-word-long code of conduct.
  • Sign into the freeCodeCamp forum, read some threads, reply to some threads, and start some threads of your own.

As you use the forum, we'll trust you with more and more power there. More people will come to recognize you as a chill person who brings useful insights.

If you're looking for an alternative to divisive social media, a place where people talk WITH each other rather than PAST each other, well this is it. You've hit the jackpot.

I'm spending a lot of time there and hope you'll do the same.

Shout out to all the mods for helping everybody get the most out of the limited minutes in their day. See you on the forum.

entries.content:
Let's say you've built a website. You've invested in the design, bought a domain, and so on. But a website isn't only what you see on the screen. A lot happens behind the scenes. You have to understand how the internet works, as well as how Search Engine Optimization (SEO) works.

Speed is a key part of it, too. A slow site can have very weak SEO, because most people won't spend much time waiting for a page to load, especially these days.

Site speed is a well-known topic with many problems of its own to consider, like Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), and server speed. But I'll leave those for another article.

This one is about the problems that stop search engines from reaching and reading your pages.

In my opinion, technical SEO is much harder to apply than regular SEO, which focuses on content and keywords. The technical side usually requires a developer's knowledge, and might need some changes that can feel a bit uncomfortable if you don't have a technical background.

A technical problem can stay unnoticed for months, because you usually don't see it. It's not a design problem. You only find it when you run specific checks, for example with Google PageSpeed Insights.

In this tutorial, you'll find and fix the most common ones on a small practice site. I didn't want to take a real website and shame its owners, so I built a practice site with the problems already in it.

Table of Contents

Prerequisites

You don't need to be an experienced programmer to follow along. You'll need:

  • A web browser, such as Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari. In Safari, first turn on Show features for web developers under Settings > Advanced.
  • A terminal: Terminal on macOS, PowerShell on Windows, or any terminal on Linux.
  • curl
    , a small program that downloads web pages. It comes with macOS, most Linux distributions, and Windows 10 (version 1803 and later) and Windows 11.
  • Node.js, to run the practice site. The code was tested with Node.js 26.8 and curl 8.7.

On Windows PowerShell, type 

curl.exe
instead of 
curl
, because there 
curl
is a shortcut to a different command. Replace 
| grep -i "text"
with 
| Select-String "text"
, and 
/dev/null
with 
NUL
.

What Is Technical SEO?

Google has programs called crawlers. They search the internet all the time for new websites and new pages. When Google discovers a new address, it may crawl the page and process what's on it (the text, images, and videos).

If Google decides the page is worth indexing, it may add it to a very big database of web pages, called the index. Google can then consider the pages in its index for its search results, when they're relevant to what someone searches for. Google's guide to how Search works calls these three steps crawling, indexing, and serving.

So crawling doesn't guarantee indexing, and indexing doesn't guarantee a place in the results. The same guide says Google doesn't guarantee any of the three stages, even for a page that follows all of its rules.

Fixing technical problems won't necessarily make your site rank first on Google. But it does strengthen your chances of ranking higher, because every problem you fix makes your site better.

Technical SEO has to come together with regular SEO, like keywords, backlinks, engagement on social media, and so on.

How Common Are These Problems on Real Websites?

The numbers below come from audits run with the site-auditing tool I build. Each website counts once, using its first audit, and this data comes from October 25th.

Crawls check many pages on one site (a median of 10 pages here). Single-page audits check one page, usually the home page.

ProblemHow oftenSample
At least one page with no canonical tag64.2% of sites53 crawled sites, Aug 2025 to Oct 2026
Two or more pages with exactly the same title61.8% of sites34 crawled sites with two or more pages that loaded
At least one page with no meta description49.1% of sites53 crawled sites
At least one link leading to a page that returns 40418.9% of sites53 crawled sites
Page built mostly with JavaScript17.7% of pages277 single-page audits, May to Oct 2026
At least one page with no title13.2% of sites53 crawled sites
A link that search engines may not be able to follow8.3% of pages278 single-page audits
A robots.txt file with errors, or one that failed to load7.9% of sites252 single-page audits, Jul to Oct 2026
Page blocked by noindex or by robots.txt4.8% of pages251 single-page audits, Jul to Oct 2026

These are all technical problems, but they don't all weigh the same. Missing canonical tags are at the top, but Google doesn't require a canonical tag, so a page without one isn't broken by itself. It matters when the same or very similar content is reachable at more than one URL, as you'll see in the canonical section.

Duplicate titles are something I had myself: when you write code, it's easy to miss things like that. That's why there are tools that check for these problems.

Let's go over each issue in the table to make sure they're all clear:

  • Missing canonical tag: a canonical tag is basically one of the many tags you put in the 
     of your HTML. When two or three pages have pretty much the same content, it tells search engines like Google which URL is the original, main version, the one you prefer to get indexed. It's not required, though: without it, Google picks the main version itself, so it matters mostly for pages that have duplicates.
  • Duplicate titles: it's really easy to end up with the same title on two pages. You don't want a duplicated title because it's not helpful and can confuse Google. Each page should say what it's about.
  • Missing meta description: this one is really important, because it helps search engines as well as AI tools like ChatGPT. The meta description is there to explain very briefly what the page is about and what it's for. If you go to Google and search for a website, you'll see it under the actual link to the site.
  • A link to a 404 page: this basically means you have a broken link (maybe a link you probably don't use anymore) to a page that isn't there. So there's no reason for it to lead to something that doesn't exist. Use it to lead to something similar, or to something that does exist, so your links remain relevant.
  • A page built mostly with JavaScript: Google can run JavaScript, so this alone doesn't keep a page out of Google. But the content appears only after the JavaScript loads and runs, which is slower for visitors and one more step that can fail, and not every crawler runs JS. That's why I prefer server-side rendering for the content that matters most.
  • A link search engines can't follow: this isn't a huge deal, and it really depends where the link goes. But say I wrote a really nice article and I want it to help me rank on Google. If search engines can't follow the link to it, then you invested all this time and energy in this article that relatively few people will likely see.
  • Errors in robots.txt: robots.txt basically helps you talk to search engines. If there are errors in this file, you might stop search engines from crawling pages you do want in search results.
  • A page blocked by noindex or robots.txt: these are two different things. A 
    noindex
     rule asks search engines to keep a page out of their results, while a robots.txt rule only stops them from crawling it. You'll learn more about both, and why the difference matters, later in this tutorial.
Soft 404s, redirect chains, and wrong canonical tags aren't in the table, because the audits don't record them.
How to Set Up the Practice Site
The practice site is a tiny website for a made-up shoe store called Acme Shoes. Every page on it has one problem built in. You don't need to understand every line of the code.
Create a new folder, add a file called 
server.js
, and paste in this code:
// server.js: a tiny practice site with common technical SEO problems built in
const http = require('node:http');

const PORT = 8080;
const BASE = 'http://localhost:' + PORT;

// Builds a simple HTML page. Leave out a field to leave that tag out.
function page({ title, description, canonical, robots, body, script }) {
  return [
    '',
    '',
    '',
    '<meta',
    title && '' + title + '',
    description && '<meta',
    canonical && '<link',
    robots && '<meta',
    '',
    '',
    body,
    script && '',
    '',
    '',
  ]
    .filter(Boolean)
    .join('\n');
}

const routes = {
  '/': {
    html: page({
      title: 'Acme Shoes: Running Shoes for Every Runner',
      description: 'Lightweight running shoes for road and trail, with free returns.',
      canonical: '/',
      body: [
        '
Acme Shoes
',
        'Blue Runner',
        'Summer sale',
      ].join('\n'),
    }),
  },
  // Problem: a vague title and no meta description
  '/products/blue-runner': {
    html: page({
      title: 'Acme Shoes',
      canonical: '/products/blue-runner',
      body: '
Blue Runner
',
    }),
  },
  // Problem: a missing product that still answers "200 OK" (a soft 404)
  '/products/red-runner': {
    html: page({
      title: 'Acme Shoes',
      body: '
Sorry, that product could not be found.
',
    }),
  },
  // Problem: a redirect chain, /old-sale -> /sale-2025 -> /sale
  '/old-sale': { redirect: '/sale-2025' },
  '/sale-2025': { redirect: '/sale' },
  '/sale': {
    html: page({
      title: 'Summer Sale: Up to 40% Off Running Shoes | Acme Shoes',
      description: "Save up to 40% on last season's running shoes until August 31.",
      canonical: '/sale',
      body: '
Summer sale
',
    }),
  },
  // Problem: a noindex header nobody can see in the page itself
  '/about': {
    headers: { 'X-Robots-Tag': 'noindex' },
    html: page({
      title: 'About Acme Shoes',
      description: 'How a two-person workshop became a running shoe brand.',
      canonical: '/about',
      body: '
About us
',
    }),
  },
  // Problem: a canonical tag that points to the home page
  '/blog/choosing-trail-shoes': {
    html: page({
      title: 'How to Choose Trail Running Shoes | Acme Shoes',
      description: 'Grip, drop and fit: what to look for in a trail running shoe.',
      canonical: '/',
      body: '
How to choose trail running shoes
',
    }),
  },
  // Problem: the content only exists after JavaScript runs
  '/catalog': {
    html: page({
      title: 'All Running Shoes | Acme Shoes',
      description: 'Browse every Acme running shoe.',
      canonical: '/catalog',
      body: '
Loading...
',
      script:
        "fetch('/api/products').then((r) => r.json()).then((products) => {" +
        "document.getElementById('app').innerHTML = products.map((p) => '
' + p + '
').join('');" +
        '});',
    }),
  },
  '/api/products': {
    type: 'application/json',
    html: JSON.stringify(['Blue Runner', 'Trail Grip 2', 'City Glide']),
  },
  // Problem: "Disallow: /blog" blocks every path that starts with /blog
  '/robots.txt': {
    type: 'text/plain',
    html: 'User-agent: *\nDisallow: /blog\n',
  },
};

http
  .createServer((req, res) => {
    const path = new URL(req.url, BASE).pathname;
    const route = routes[path];

    if (!route) {
      res.writeHead(404, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8' });
      return res.end(page({ title: 'Page not found', body: '
Page not found
' }));
    }
    if (route.redirect) {
      res.writeHead(301, { Location: route.redirect });
      return res.end();
    }
    res.writeHead(200, {
      'Content-Type': (route.type || 'text/html') + '; charset=utf-8',
      ...route.headers,
    });
    res.end(route.html);
  })
  .listen(PORT, () => console.log('Practice site running at ' + BASE));



Each key in 
routes
 is a page address. The comments that start with 
Problem:
 say what's wrong with each page.
Start the server from the same folder:
node server.js



You should see:
Practice site running at http://localhost:8080



Leave the server running and open a second terminal for the commands below. When you change 
server.js
, stop the server with Ctrl+C and start it again.
How to Check a Page's HTTP Status Code
I remember when I started building websites, I built all kinds of small things. I'm a full stack developer, and I kept trying experiments.
Once I had a problem on the server side and saw in the Network tab that it returned a 500 error. Another time I removed a page on purpose, because I wanted to see if I'd get a 404 or other problems. If you just play around with the site you're building, you'll learn a lot from the results.
HTTP status codes are the first thing a search engine reads. They're the server's way of talking to the client, such as your browser. The codes are split into five ranges: 1xx, 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx. A 5xx code is a server problem, for example, and a 4xx code is a client-side problem.
404 is the most common error. It means a page on the site wasn't found. You see 404s all the time, and the fix is typically just to maintain your site and your links.
The codes you'll see in this tutorial are:
  • 200 OK
    : here's the page.
  • 301 Moved Permanently
    : the page lives at another address.
  • 404 Not Found
    : there's no page here.
Google doesn't index URLs that return a 
4xx
 code, according to its documentation on HTTP status codes.
To see the status code of the practice site's home page, use 
-I
, which shows only the headers, and 
-s
, which hides curl's progress meter:
curl -sI http://localhost:8080/



HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:42:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5



Now ask for an address that isn't in 
routes
, to see what a correct 404 looks like:
curl -sI http://localhost:8080/products/does-not-exist



HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:42:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5



In the browser, open the developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac), go to the Network tab, and reload. The Status column shows the code.
What Is a Soft 404?
Check a product the store no longer sells:
curl -sI http://localhost:8080/products/red-runner



HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:42:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5



In the browser, the same page says "Sorry, that product could not be found."
A soft 404 is basically a "page not found", but the server still answers 
200
. It confuses Google, because the address is still there, but what's on it isn't current anymore.
To fix it, make missing pages return a real 
404
, which is what Google recommends. In the practice site, delete the 
'/products/red-runner'
 entry from 
routes
. The server then answers 
404
.
Broken links lead to the same dead end. In the data, 18.9% of the 53 crawled sites had at least one link to a page that returned 
404
.
So don't leave links that lead to something that doesn't exist. Update them to lead to something similar, or to something that does exist.
If the page moved, add a 
301
 redirect from the old address to the new one. A 
404
 is the right answer only for a page that's really gone.
How to Find and Fix Redirect Chains
A redirect is basically when you want to send one URL (perhaps one that no longer exists) to another URL (that does exist). You might set up a redirect if, for example, you change your domain from 
example-x.com
 to 
example-y.com
. You'll want everyone who types 
example-x.com
 to be redirected to 
example-y.com
 automatically.
Redirects are fine, and they can be quite helpful when used properly. A 
301
 means the page moved for good. A 
302
 means the move is temporary. Google's documentation on redirects explains how it treats each one, and its crawlers follow up to 10 redirect hops.
But a redirect chain happens when an old address, such as a domain you used in the past, redirects to a new one, and then that one redirects again, and again...you get the picture. A few redirects aren't a big deal, but five, six, or seven can be a real problem.
The first command below shows every step of the chain. The second gives you a one-line summary.
Add 
-L
 so curl follows the redirects:
curl -sIL http://localhost:8080/old-sale



HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /sale-2025
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:42:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /sale
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:42:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:42:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5



/old-sale
 goes to 
/sale-2025
, which goes to 
/sale
. For a one-line summary:
curl -sL -o /dev/null -w "%{num_redirects} redirects, ended at %{url_effective}\n" http://localhost:8080/old-sale



2 redirects, ended at http://localhost:8080/sale



-o /dev/null
 tells curl to write the page's HTML nowhere, so it doesn't fill your terminal and only the summary line is printed. 
-w
 sets what that summary line says.
To fix it, point the old/original address straight at the final page:
'/old-sale': { redirect: '/sale' },



Restart the server and run the summary again. It now says 
1 redirects, ended at http://localhost:8080/sale
.
How to Make Sure robots.txt Isn't Blocking Important Pages
robots.txt is the site's way of telling search engines like Google (and their crawlers) what they're allowed to explore and where they have access.
Look at the practice site's file:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/robots.txt



User-agent: *
Disallow: /blog



Disallow: /blog
 is dangerous because it stops crawlers from reading every path that starts with 
/blog
. And usually, your articles are what promote your site the most.
Google's robots.txt documentation gives the same kind of example: 
Disallow: /fish
 also blocks 
/fish.html
 and 
/fishheads
.
To fix it, make the rule match only what you meant to block, for example a folder of drafts:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /blog-drafts/



In the practice site, change the 
html
 line of the 
'/robots.txt'
 entry:
html: 'User-agent: *\nDisallow: /blog-drafts/\n',



robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing. Google says it's not a mechanism for keeping a page out of Google. For that, you need 
noindex
.
A URL blocked in robots.txt can even appear in search results, usually without a description, if other pages link to it. Google just never reads what's on the page.
How to Find an Accidental noindex
noindex
 tells Google not to index a particular page. It's harmful when it ends up on pages you do want indexed and ranked, like a product page or your home page.
But it can be useful on pages you don't need to rank for, or that don't add much to the site, such as log in, sign in, and sign up pages.
noindex
 works only when the crawler can reach the page and read the rule. If robots.txt blocks the same URL, Google never sees the 
noindex
, and the page can still show up in search results. So for a page you want out of Google, use 
noindex
 and leave the page crawlable.
In the data, 11 of 457 audited pages (2.4%) had a 
noindex
 robots meta tag. There are two ways to set it, and you need to check both.
How to Check the Robots Meta Tag
The first way is a tag in the page's 
:
<meta



Search the page for the word:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/about | grep -i noindex



On the About page, this prints nothing. You can also right-click the page, choose View Page Source, and search for 
noindex
.
Fixing a noindex is really easy. You basically remove it, and then search engines can index the page.
Look for it in the page's code or template, and in your CMS or SEO plugin settings. In WordPress, the setting Discourage search engines from indexing this site adds it to every page.
How to Check the X-Robots-Tag Header
The second way is an HTTP header. Check the About page's headers:
curl -sI http://localhost:8080/about



HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

The header doesn't appear in View Page Source, only in the response headers. In the data, 5 of the 12 blocked pages had no 
noindex
 in their HTML: 2 had this header, and 3 were blocked from crawling by robots.txt.
To fix it in the practice site, delete the 
headers
 line from the 
'/about'
 entry. On a real site, check the server configuration, the hosting provider's header settings, and any SEO plugin.
How to Use Canonical Tags Correctly
If you have several pages that talk about more or less the same thing, but without enough meat to be different, you want to designate one main page. The canonical tag tells search engines which page that is.
The same page can also live at several addresses:
https://example.com/blog/choosing-trail-shoes
https://example.com/blog/choosing-trail-shoes?utm_source=newsletter
https://www.example.com/blog/choosing-trail-shoes



These three addresses show the same article. The first one is the main one: the address you want Google to show in search results. So all three carry the same canonical tag, pointing to that main page:
<link



When Google sees this tag on the 
?utm_source=newsletter
 version, it knows that page is a copy of the first address. The main address carries the same tag, pointing to itself. That's called a self-referencing canonical, and it says: I'm the main version.
Google treats it as a strong signal, not a command. If you use canonical tags, a self-referencing one on each main page is a good practice, and Google recommends it.
But you don't have to use canonical tags at all. Google says specifying a canonical isn't required: without one, it picks the version it thinks is best to show users. A canonical tag is a good choice when the same or very similar content is reachable at more than one URL, like the three addresses above.
That's why a missing canonical tag isn't a defect by itself. In the data, 27.1% of 457 audited pages had no canonical tag. What matters is whether any of them have duplicates, like a version with tracking parameters, that need one.
Check the practice site's trail shoe article:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/blog/choosing-trail-shoes | grep -i canonical



<link



The article says its main version is the home page, so Google may show the home page instead of it, or ignore the tag.
The article isn't a copy of anything, so it's its own main version. To fix it, point the article's canonical tag to the article itself:
canonical: '/blog/choosing-trail-shoes',



How to Fix Missing and Duplicate Titles and Meta Descriptions
A good title or meta description is the right length, isn't overloaded, and says briefly what the page is about. It's sort of the essence of the page, like its introduction.
Look at the Blue Runner product page:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/products/blue-runner | grep -i -E "|name=\"description\""
</pre></pre>
<pre><pre><title>Acme Shoes



The title says nothing about the page, and there's no description line at all. In PowerShell, use 
| Select-String '|name="description"'</pre> for this one.<p>Google's guides to <a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link">titles</a> and <a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/snippet">snippets</a> ask for a unique, descriptive title and description on every page.</p><p>To fix it in the practice site, replace the </p><pre>title</pre> line of the <pre>'/products/blue-runner'</pre> entry with:<pre><pre>title: 'Blue Runner Road Running Shoe | Acme Shoes',
description: 'A lightweight road running shoe with a cushioned sole and free returns.',
</pre></pre>
<h2>How to Make Your Links Crawlable</h2><p>Look at the practice site's home page:</p><pre><pre>curl -s http://localhost:8080/
</pre></pre>
<pre><pre><!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta
<title>Acme Shoes: Running Shoes for Every Runner
<meta
<link



Acme Shoes

Blue Runner
Summer sale





Everything else on this page is fine: the title, the description, the canonical tag and the Blue Runner link, which is a real 
 element with an 
href
. The only problem is the "Summer sale" 
.
A 
 is basically HTML that isn't semantic, meaning it has no meaning. A real link does have meaning: search engines can understand it's a link, and screen readers can understand it's a link.
Which links need to be crawlable? Basically, everything you want search engines to see. I mean the products you sell, your articles, your courses, and other things like that.
Google's link guidelines say it can only reliably crawl an 
 element with an 
href
.
To fix it in the practice site, replace the 
 line with:
'Summer sale',



How to Check Whether Your Content Needs JavaScript to Appear
With client-side rendering, the JavaScript has to load first, and only then can the other content load.
JavaScript usually builds things like product lists, prices, reviews and menus. Without it, a client-side page often shows only a loading message or an empty box.
Google does render JavaScript, but in a later phase. The page waits in a rendering queue, which can take a few seconds or longer, and a script that fails or is blocked can leave the rendered page without its content.
That's why server-side rendering is still a good idea, and it's what I prefer for the content that matters. Google's JavaScript guide says the same: server-side rendering makes the site faster for users and crawlers, and not all bots can run JavaScript.
In the data, 17.7% of 277 audited pages were built mostly with JavaScript. That doesn't mean Google couldn't index them, only that their main content depended on JavaScript running correctly.
With server-side rendering, the HTML content comes straight to the browser, and only after that does the JavaScript render.
Google can index pages built either way. Its crawler runs JavaScript with an up-to-date version of Chrome, so server-side rendering isn't a requirement for getting into Google's index.
The next test checks whether the important content is visible without JavaScript. It doesn't show what Google sees, because Google runs the JavaScript, but it shows what every crawler gets before any JavaScript runs.
Open 
http://localhost:8080/catalog
 in your browser. You'll see three products. Now download it with curl, which doesn't run JavaScript:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/catalog | grep -i "trail grip"



This prints nothing, because the product names aren't in the HTML the server sends. Inside 
, the server only sends:
Loading...





Without curl, use View Page Source in your browser. On this page, you'll see "Loading..." and the script, but none of the product names, because the browser adds them only after the JavaScript runs.
On your own site, search the source for an important sentence from the page.
To see the page the way Google renders it, use Google's own tools on a live page. On your own site, the URL Inspection tool in Search Console can run a live test (Test live URL, then View tested page) and show the HTML Google rendered and a screenshot.
For any public page, the Rich Results Test shows the rendered HTML too. Google recommends both for finding JavaScript problems. Neither can reach 
localhost
, so try them on your real site.
If you want the product names in the HTML from the start, render them on the server. In the practice site, add the product list above 
routes
:
const products = ['Blue Runner', 'Trail Grip 2', 'City Glide'];



Replace the catalog's 
body
 and 
script
 lines with:
body: '
' + products.map((p) => '
' + p + '
').join('') + '
',



And in the 
'/api/products'
 entry:
html: JSON.stringify(products),



Restart the server and run the curl command again:
Blue Runner
Trail Grip 2
City Glide




This works because the server now writes the product names into the HTML before it sends the page. Any crawler sees them, even one that can't run JavaScript, and you can still use JavaScript for the interactive parts.
Can You Check a Page in Five Minutes?
Honestly, it's very hard. There can be a lot of problems, and five minutes isn't enough.
To really know what the problems are, you need to run a full check, for example in Google PageSpeed Insights. If the site is yours, also use the URL Inspection tool in Google Search Console.
The commands from this tutorial are a good start:
  • curl -sI
     for the status code and an 
    X-Robots-Tag
     header.
  • curl -sIL
     on an old address to count redirects.
  • /robots.txt
    , line by line.
  • View Page Source for 
    noindex
    , 
    canonical
    , 
    </pre>, <pre>description</pre> and your important content.</li></ul><h2>Conclusion</h2><p>In this tutorial, you fixed eight problems on a practice site: a soft 404, a redirect chain, a robots.txt rule, a hidden </p><pre>noindex</pre> header, a wrong canonical tag, a vague title and a missing description, a link crawlers couldn't follow, and content that needed JavaScript.<p>The most important thing to remember is that you'll need to check your site all the time. Run scans, do maintenance, and make sure nothing breaks, especially when you make improvements or changes to the site.</p><p>If you want to go further, my tutorial on <a href="https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/nextjs-json-ld-structured-data/">adding structured data (JSON-LD) to a Next.js site</a> is a good next step.</p><p>If you'd like to check a live page for many of these issues in one go, my free tool <a href="https://www.greadme.com/page-audit">Greadme Page Audit</a> tests any URL with no sign-up needed.</p>

entries.title: How to Automate Docker Image Creation for Postgres Using Shell Commands
entries.summary: If you have certain lines of code that repeat over and over again in a project, there's a pretty standard solution for it: using a function. But what about when you have the same project file setup th
entries.content:
If you have certain lines of code that repeat over and over again in a project, there's a pretty standard solution for it: using a function.

But what about when you have the same project file setup that gets repeated over and over? How do you solve that?

Meet bash scripting. Bash scripts are written to execute certain sequences of commands on your machine automatically without you having to do anything. This is known as workflow automation, and that's what I'll be teaching you how to do in this article.

Table Of Contents

Prerequisites

To follow along with this article, you should have:

  • Git-bash installed on your machine
  • Some experience using a terminal or command prompt to run and execute commands (helpful but not required)
  • Understanding of basic programming concepts (like conditions and loops)
  • Docker installed on your machine
  • Basic understanding of Docker concepts (like images and containers)
  • Experience using Postgres (optional but recommended)

What Motivated This Project?

I was recently setting up a Docker image for Postgres on a few projects I was working on, and I noticed that I was following the same pattern in creating the images. The only difference was that they had different database credentials and database names.

I also realized that a large portion of today's rapidly developed apps tend to use Supabase as their backend, which can come with resource limits such as database storage, bandwidth, concurrent connections, and API request quotas (depending on the service tier and size of the project). And these issues can be solved by setting up your database.

So I thought, why not make a CLI tool that could automate creating Docker images for Postgres? That's when I learned about writing executable shell commands using bash to create workflow automations.

You can find the full working example used in this guide in this git-repo.

Introduction

Bash is a shell and scripting language used to write and execute commands or scripts that perform operations on a computer, such as creating directories and files, manipulating files, automating tasks, and managing system processes.

In this guide, you'll learn to automate the process of creating a Docker image for a Postgres database so that you don't have to create the image from scratch for each new project.

Bash Scripting File Setup

To get started, open you preferred text-editor and create a directory or folder there. Then within that directory, create a file with the extension 

.sh
.

At the beginning of a file, type:

#!/bin/bash


#!/bin/bash
(known as a "shebang") tells the operating system to run the script using the Bash shell, so the commands inside the file are executed as Bash/terminal commands.

Conditions in bash

After you've finished creating a script file and adding shebang, let's start by exploring how if statements are used in bash.

The syntax of 

if
looks like this:
if [[ condition ]];
    then
        command to execute
fi

The 

if
in bash is no different from what you're used to in other programming languages:
  • You use double square braces ([]) to add a condition you're checking against and a semicolon (;).
  • You use 
    then
    after the 
    if
    declaration to specify what should be executed if the condition is true.
  • You use the 
    fi
    to close the condition statement.

When you're writing the condition inside the square braces, make sure you leave a space before the condition and another one after it (as you can see in the code above). If you omit these spaces, you'll get errors.

Working Example:

Since we are automating Postgres database Docker image creation, first check if the file exists and has content. If it does have content, end the script. If not, we'll proceed with the next script.

#!/bin/bash

if [[ -s docker-compose.yml ]];
    then
        echo "The file already exists"
        exit 0
fi

echo "Next command"

In the if condition, we use the flag 

-s
to check if the file exists and has contents. File flags check file availability and permissions, and include but aren't limited to:
  • -f: used to check if the file exists
  • -s: used to check if the file exists and has contents
  • -d: used to check if a directory exists
  • -r: used to check if a file is readable
  • -w: used to check if a file is writable
  • -x: used to check if a file is executable

In the script, we're using 

-s
to check if a file named 
docker-compose.yml
exists in the directory where we're executing the command. If it's false, we use the 
echo
keyword to print the text "Next command". If it's true, we print the text "The file already exists".

exit
acts as a return keyword for bash scripting, 0 is used for success, and 1 is used for failure.

Let's test all this by creating a Docker Compose file and adding some content in the same directory where we're writing the bash script. In your terminal type 

bash name-of-file.sh
, and you should see "The file already exists":

But if we delete the content in the file and run the command again, we should see the output saying "Next command":

Interactive Shell

To make an automation dynamic and flexible you will need to receive inputs, take an example of a database name you won't always have the same database name, the name will change based on the project,

you do need to setup away to use a given name of the database when creating a new docker image for that you read inputs using the 

read
keyword.

There are different types of inputs based on the operation. And there are flags that are used to specify which type of input you're expecting, such as:

  • -p: for prompting the user to write a text
  • -s: used on passwords when you want the user input to stay hidden when writing it in the terminal
  • -a: used when you're expecting the user to pass in multiple inputs or if you're expecting an array from user.

Here's the syntax for reading user input:

read -p 'input_label: ' variable_name

Working Example:

Now let's create scripts to receive user input about the Postgres database image you're going to create.

#!/bin/bash

# database credentials
read -p 'DataBase-name(*): ' db
read -p 'DataBase-user(*): ' user
read -sp 'DataBase-password(*): ' pwd
echo
echo "your database is -> $db with a username of $user and a password of $pwd"

The script uses 

-p
on the 
read
keyword that prompts a string of text and 
-sp
that prompts the user to enter a string of text that's hidden (because the 
-s
hides what's being typed).

If you don't use the 

-p
option together with 
-s
, you won't be able to display a prompt asking the user to enter a password. With 
-s
alone, the input is hidden, but no prompt is shown unless you print one using 
echo
or 
printf
.

To print or use the input the user has added, use the dollar sign ($) followed with a variable name for the input you're expecting from the user. In the example above, we named the variable for getting the database name 

db
, so we'll use 
$db
when we want to access the name of the database the user has input.

Now if you run the script in the terminal, you should see a sequence of terminal prompts waiting for inputs. Once they're filled, you'll see all the input's values in the terminal:

How to Validate and Sanitize Input

You'll also need to validate input before executing anything. This is important because sometimes crucial field might be missing or mistyped. For example, you might forget to input the database name for the image you're trying to create.

When validating input, you'll use one of these flags (among others):

  • -z: checks if a variable value is empty
  • -n: checks if a variable value is not empty
  • -lt: checks if a number is less than a given number
  • -gt: checks if a number is greater than a given number
  • -eq: checks for equality of two values

You can use the 

-z
flag on every input that you need to make sure isn't empty before moving on to the next step:
#!/bin/bash

# database credentials
read -p 'DataBase-name(*): ' db
if [[ -z $db ]]
    then
        echo "The database field cannot be empty!"
        exit 1
fi

read -p 'DataBase-user(*): ' user
if [[ -z $user ]]
    then
        echo "The user field cannot be empty!"
        exit 1
fi

read -sp 'DataBase-password(*): ' pwd
if [[ -z $pwd ]]
    then
        echo "The password field cannot be empty!"
        exit 1
fi

This script helps you make sure that all critical information about the database is present before proceeding to another input.

Default Values

You may want some fields to use default value (for example, the container name of the image, port, or volume of the container). For such scenarios you can use 

:=
to assign a variable default value:
#!/bin/bash

# container information
read -p 'Container-name: ' container_name
read -p 'Container-port(if omitted, the container will use default postgresql default port of 5432): ' port
read -p 'Volume-name: ' vol_name

echo "container-name-> ${container_name:=cont_one}, port->${port:=5432}, volume_name->${vol_name:=backend_data}"

When you run the script and skip all three of those inputs, bash will use the default value(s) you've used as fallbacks.

But if you pass value for those inputs, bash uses the provided values. For example, supply all three inputs and see the output you get:

How to Create and Write to a File

Now that you know how to create a Docker image for a Postgres database, you need to create a 

docker-compose.yml
file that will be executed when starting and stopping your containers.

In Bash, there are multiple ways of creating a file:

  • First, you can use 
    > filename
    . This creates a file if it doesn't exist. If it exists, its contents are overwritten (replaced).
  • There's also 
    >> filename
    : This appends contents to a file or creates a file if one doesn't exist.
  • Finally, there's 
    touch filename
    : This creates a file if it doesn't exist. If the file already exists, its contents are preserved and only the file's timestamps are updated.

How to Use 
>
to Create and Write to a File

When you want to create a file and write content to it at the same time, you'll want to use echo in front of 

>
and then add the filename, like this:
#!/bin/bash

echo Hello> test.txt

This will create a 

test.txt
file with "hello" as content inside.

How to Use 
>>
to Append Contents to an Existing File

To append contents to an existing file, add the contents before the 

>>
and then follow with the filename you want to append content onto. Let's add Africa after Hello in the 
test.txt
file we created in the previous script.
#!/bin/bash

echo Africa!>> test.txt

Now test.txt will have Hello and Africa! on the new line.

Using those symbols, let's create a 

docker-compose.yml
file that will hold contents about our Postgres database setup.
#!/bin/bash

> docker-compose.yml

And just like that you have your docker-compose file created in your directory.

How to Write Multiple Different Contents to a File

You can also use the 

cat
keyword to write to a file. Typically, 
cat
is used for reading the contents of a file. But when you combine it with 
< and the sign for appending contents to a file 
>>
 (that we just discussed), you can add multiple contents to a file in the format you want. The syntax looks like this:
# writing docker compose contents

cat <> docker-compose.yml

  # file contents
EOF



The 
< tells bash to write contents to a file until it finds the EOF keyword (end of file). Then you use 
>> filename
 to append the contents to the file. With a Docker compose setup it would look like this:
#!/bin/bash

#file creation and writing
 >  docker-compose.yml

cat<>docker-compose.yml
 services:
    postgres:
        image: postgres:18-alpine
        container_name: ${container_name:= $db}

        environment:
            POSTGRES_USER: $user
            POSTGRES_PASSWORD: $pwd
            POSTGRES_database: $db

        ports:
            - ${port:=5432}:5432
        volumes:
            - ${vol_name:=database-data}:/var/postgresql

 volumes:
    ${vol_name:=database-data}:

EOF



Bash Arguments and Flags
With Bash arguments, you can pass values in the same line while executing a script. To use arguments, add the values while executing the script on the same line, like this:
bash script val1 val2 



To read arguments value(s), use the dollar sign ($) followed by the position in which you inputted your values (positions start at 1, not 0).
In the example, if you want to echo the content of the second argument value, you can use 
echo $2
.
To understand this better, let's enhance data input experience by passing the database credentials on the fly using arguments:
#!/bin/bash

# database credentials

if [[ -z $1 ]]; then
    read -p 'DataBase-name(*): ' db
 else
    db="$1"
fi

# database checking and validating

if [[ -z $2 ]]; then
    read -p 'DataBase-user(*): ' user
 else
    user="$2"
fi

# user checking and validating

if [[ -z $1 ]]; then
    read -sp 'DataBase-password(*): ' pwd
 else
    pwd=$3
fi

# password vaidation and checking



The snippet first checks if there's an argument. If there aren't any, you use the prompt to input the value. If there are arguments, you assign the argument value to a variable that represents the given database credentials (database name, password, and so on...). Now you can run the script with arguments:
bash image.sh customers ABC-Company secret123!



The image that will be created from the above script will have a database of 
customers
, user 
ABC-Company
, and a password of 
secret123!
.
Bash Flags/Options
The script has a section that asks for information about the image that you're creating, but the info can be optional. With bash option/flags, you can skip the step that prompts for container information input using the 
-D
 option. This lets you explicitly keep the default container info before the script runs.
Here's an example:
#!/bin/bash

while getopts "ny" options; do
	case "$options" in
		n) echo "You choose no";;
		y) echo "You choose yes";;
		*) echo "No such option/flag"; exit 1;;
    esac
done

shift $((OPTIND - 1))



In the above script:
  • The while loop keeps running as long as 
    getopts
     isn't empty
  • getopts
     gets the passed option in the script
  • "ny"
     are the options we're expecting from user when running the script
  • options
     is a variable that will keep track of the input option between "n" and "y"
  • do
     starts the loop
  • case
     checks if the selected option is in the defined option using the 
    in
     keyword
  • We then define what happens when we call the script with the option 
    -n
     or 
    -y
     and use a double semi-colon (;;) to close the option definition
  • The 
    *
     is used in case the input options aren't defined.
  • esac
     then closes the case
  • done
     ends the loop so the loop doesn't continue running forever
  • shift $((OPTIND - 1))
     helps avoid a conflict that may occur when the script also expects arguments by shifting the remaining arguments left over the flags, effectively discarding the flags from the parameter list.
You can then apply the syntax in the script to skip the step that asks for container info when 
-D
 is passed as an option during the script execution.
#!/bin/bash

ask_container_info=true

while getopts "D" options; do
	case "$options" in
		D) ask_container_info=false;;
		*) echo "No such option/flag"; exit 1;;
    esac
done

shift $((OPTIND - 1))

if [[ $ask_container_info == true ]]; then
	#Prompt the user to input custom container information
    read -p 'Container-name: ' container_name
    read -p 'Container-port(if omitted, the container will use default postgresql default port of 5432): ' port
    read -p 'Volume-name: ' vol_name
fi



There is one option here, which is why the option section only has 
D
. 
ask_container_info
 starts as true, meaning unless the option is passed, the script will prompt the user to enter the container information. We then change the value of 
ask_container_info
 to false when the 
-D
 is passed with the script's execution.
How to Make Your Scripts Executable and Available on Your PC's Path
The next step is to make the script available and executable in every terminal you use on your machine. At the moment, the script just works in the current directory you're using to create and write your scripts.
We'll start by making the script file executable and remove the file extension from the file, so we don't need to always call our script with the 
.sh
 extension.
How to Make a File Executable
To make a file executable, use the Linux 
chmod
 command. It stands for change mode. Mode includes file permissions like write, read, and execute.
chmod +x image



Here, 
x
 makes the file executable, and then you've listed the file name you want to make executable (
image
).
How to Add Your Directory to the 
system/machine
 Path


To make this available in every terminal you open, regardless of the directory, you'll need to register your scripts in the system paths where all global scripts and commands are stored.
To do that, copy the full path of your directory and then in your terminal type the following:
export PATH="$PATH:"



Replace 
 with your directory. This command will add the script directory into the current working terminal. But if you try to switch to another terminal and run your script, it'll fail.
Now let's configure the directory globally so every terminal will be able to execute the script:
nano ~/.bash_profile



After this you should see something that looks like this:
You can see in the image above that I already have my path declared in the file (see the selected text).
If it's not in you're file, you can copy-paste 
export PATH="$PATH:"
 inside the file. When you're done, press 
Ctrl+O
 and then 
enter
 to save. Then press 
Ctrl+x
 to exit the nano editor.
Then re-load the machine path again to include your scripts there:
source ~/.bash_profile



After this, you'll be able to run your script in any terminal on your machine using the script file name only (I named my file 
image
):
Conclusion
In this guide, you learned how to create your own scripts to automate your workflows. I hope it helps you reduce the amount of energy and time you waste on repetitive tasks that can be automated using script commands.
You can find the full working CLI tool that we used as an example in this guide on this git-repo. There you'll find the installation guide and usage tips. If you find it helpful, please consider starring the repo and sharing it with your collogues who might benefit from it.
Thanks!

entries.title: How to Partner with Design Studios on Client Builds: A Freelance Developer's Guide
